cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Access Has a Price
cards.instruction: Turn every piece of access, information, or approval into a favor, debt, or condition.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. I'll unlock the storeroom if you cover my reception break.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Someone spilled coffee in the lobby. Just tell me where the mop is.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. Behind the buckets. That's five minutes of cover; unlocking costs another ten.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Lend me the key. I'll mop first, then cover your break.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: The key costs tomorrow's break too. Today's cover pays for opening the door.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 sets access terms, A3 unilaterally prices even mop location and A5 distinguishes key privilege from door service, making assumed superior approval control each transaction.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 shortcut information request causes A3 new fee; B4 delayed cover/key offer causes A5 extra future cover. Timing remains proposed rather than a claim that B covers reception while mopping.

relationship.evidence: B2 has a real lobby spill and B4 offers to complete both tasks in order, so A prices a practical solution rather than an arbitrary objection.

heightening.evidence: B4 request for portable access causes A5 a second-day price distinct from today door opening.

specificity.evidence: A1 storeroom and B2 mop explain the access need; A3 buckets are a location answer, and B4 key would permit entry.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 today pays only for opening makes every simplification a new product, earned by B4 key request.
